title: OST2 Arch1001 06: Function Parameter Passing and Calling Conventions (part 1 of 2)

questions.q: Under the Microsoft x64 ABI (Visual Studio), which register carries the FIRST integer/pointer argument to a function?
choices: RDI
RCX
RAX
R8
questions.explain: The Microsoft x64 ABI passes arguments 1-4 in RCX, RDX, R8 and R9. RDI is the first-argument register under System V, not Microsoft.

questions.q: Under the System V x86-64 ABI (GCC/Clang on Linux, the BSDs and macOS), what is the order of the six registers used for the first six integer arguments?
choices: RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9
RCX, RDX, R8, R9, RDI, RSI
RSI, RDI, RCX, RDX, R8, R9
RDI, RSI, RCX, RDX, R8, R9
questions.explain: System V: arg1 RDI, arg2 RSI, arg3 RDX, arg4 RCX, arg5 R8, arg6 R9. RDX comes before RCX, which is the reverse of the Microsoft order for those two.

questions.q: func(a, b, c, d, e) is compiled by Visual Studio for x64. Which 64-bit register holds d when func is entered?
questions.explain: a goes in RCX, b in RDX, c in R8 and d in R9. e goes on the stack. In TooManyParameters, main did 'mov r9d,44h' for d.

questions.q: The same func(a, b, c, d, e) is compiled by GCC for Linux x86-64. Where is e passed?
choices: R8
R9
On the stack, above the shadow store
RCX
questions.explain: System V: a goes in RDI, b in RSI, c in RDX, d in RCX and e in R8. Five arguments fit in System V's six argument registers, so this 'too many parameters' case isn't too many there, and System V has no shadow store.

questions.q: A function takes 8 integer parameters and is compiled for the System V x86-64 ABI. How many of those parameters are passed on the stack rather than in registers?
questions.explain: System V passes six in registers (RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9), so parameters 7 and 8 go on the stack. Under the Microsoft x64 ABI, 4 of the 8 would go on the stack.

questions.q: A function returns a 128-bit value. Which register holds the upper 64 bits?
choices: RAX
RDX
RCX
RBX
questions.explain: 128-bit values come back in RDX:RAX, with RDX holding the top 64 bits and RAX the bottom 64. Anything 64 bits or smaller comes back in RAX alone.

questions.q: When arguments beyond the register-passed ones go on the stack (in either 64-bit ABI), how are they laid out?
choices: The leftmost stack argument ends up at the lowest address, and compilers usually write them with mov rather than push
The rightmost stack argument ends up at the lowest address, and they are always written with push
They are placed in the order the callee first uses them
They are placed below the return address, inside the callee's own frame
questions.explain: They are notionally 'pushed' in reverse order so the leftmost ends up lowest. In practice the compiler usually stores them with mov (e.g. mov qword ptr [rsp+20h],55h).

questions.q: Both the Microsoft x64 and System V x86-64 ABIs pass parameters in a subset of the caller-save (volatile) registers.
questions.explain: Both ABIs pass arguments and return values in caller-save registers: RAX for the return value, plus RCX/RDX/R8/R9 (MS) or RDI/RSI/RDX/RCX/R8/R9 (System V).

questions.q: A calling convention has two main parts. Which pair are they?
choices: Register conventions (which registers belong to the caller vs. the callee) and parameter-passing conventions (how arguments go in and return values come out)
Instruction encoding and memory addressing modes
Heap allocation rules and stack allocation rules
Exception handling and thread-local storage
questions.explain: Both parts are compiler-dependent. The course covers the Microsoft x64 ABI (Visual Studio) and the System V x86-64 ABI (GCC/Clang).

questions.q: Because calling conventions are compiler-dependent, code from two different compilers can be mutually incompatible unless one deliberately follows the other's convention.
questions.explain: An ABI (Application Binary Interface) is the standard for how executables should work on an architecture. Unless a compiler deliberately follows another's convention (e.g. GCC targeting Microsoft code), they can generate incompatible code.

questions.q: Microsoft calls caller-save registers 'volatile'. What does that tell the caller?
choices: It should assume the callee will change them, so it must save any value it still needs before the call and restore it afterward
It can assume the callee will leave them unchanged
The callee may only read them, never write them
The call instruction resets them to zero
questions.explain: Caller-save registers 'belong' to the callee, which may smash them freely. If the caller needs a value afterward, it saves the register before the call and restores it after.

questions.q: Callee-save (non-volatile) registers are said to 'belong' to the callee.
questions.explain: They belong to the caller. The caller assumes they won't change, so a callee that wants to use them must save and restore them. Caller-save registers are the ones that 'belong' to the callee.

questions.q: Which of these are caller-save (volatile) registers in the Visual Studio x64 convention?
choices: RAX
RBX
RCX
RSI
RDI
questions.explain: Visual Studio's caller-save registers are RAX, RCX, RDX and R8-R11. Its callee-save registers are RBX, RBP, RDI, RSI and R12-R15.

questions.q: The register-saving rules of Visual Studio x64 and GCC/System V x86-64 differ only for which registers?
choices: RSI and RDI
RBX and RBP
R10 and R11
RAX and RDX
questions.explain: Visual Studio treats RSI/RDI as callee-save. System V treats them as caller-save, and they are its 1st and 2nd argument registers. All other registers are classified the same way.

questions.q: Which of these are callee-save registers under the System V (GCC) x86-64 convention?
choices: RBX
RBP
RSI
RDI
questions.explain: System V callee-save registers are RBX, RBP and R12-R15. RSI and RDI are caller-save in System V (they carry arguments 1 and 2), and R11 is caller-save in both conventions.

questions.q: While reading disassembly you see a few registers pushed immediately before a call and popped, balanced, immediately after it. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The caller is saving caller-save registers it needs after the call
The callee is saving callee-save registers
Those registers are being passed as arguments
The compiler is setting up a frame pointer
questions.explain: Callers typically save right before the call and restore right after it. Callees typically save at the start of the function and restore at the end. To confirm, check the registers against the caller-save list.

questions.q: In MS x64 code, a function begins by pushing RBX and R12 and ends with matching pops just before ret. What is happening?
choices: The callee is preserving non-volatile (callee-save) registers it intends to use
The caller is preserving volatile registers across a call
RBX and R12 are being passed as the 5th and 6th arguments
The function is allocating shadow space
questions.explain: RBX and R12 are callee-save. Saving them at the start and restoring them at the end is the callee pattern, and the balanced push/pop keeps the caller's values intact.

questions.q: What is the Microsoft x64 'shadow store' (shadow space)?
choices: Stack space the caller reserves so the callee can save the four register parameters (RCX, RDX, R8, R9) if it wants
A copy of the callee's local variables kept for the debugger
A hidden register bank that mirrors RCX, RDX, R8 and R9
Space the callee reserves in its own frame for its return value
questions.explain: The x64 ABI uses a four-register fast-call convention. Space is allocated on the call stack as a shadow store so callees can save those registers.

questions.q: How many bytes is the shadow store that a Visual Studio x64 caller reserves? (decimal)
questions.explain: 4 registers x 8 bytes = 32 bytes (0x20). This is the 'hex 20 chunk' that shows up right above the return address.

questions.q: The caller only reserves shadow space when the callee actually takes four or more parameters.
questions.explain: The caller must always allocate space for four register parameters, even if the callee takes fewer. The compiler reserves it even when no parameters are passed, as in CallASubroutine1's func().

questions.q: Who writes the register parameters into the shadow space?
choices: The callee, if it needs to (e.g. func storing ECX to [rsp+8] on entry)
The caller, always, right before the call
The CPU, automatically, as part of the call instruction
Nobody; the space is reserved but must never be written
questions.explain: 'The callee has the responsibility of dumping the register parameters into their shadow space if needed.' That's why func reaches up into main's frame.

questions.q: In CallASubroutine1, main() calls func() with no arguments and has no locals, yet starts with sub rsp,28h. What makes up that 0x28?
choices: 0x20 bytes of shadow store plus 8 bytes of padding to keep the stack 16-byte aligned
0x28 bytes reserved for main's return value
Five 8-byte slots for possible arguments
8 bytes for a saved RBP plus 0x20 bytes of locals
questions.explain: The expanded stack diagram shows the return address, then 16-byte-alignment padding, then RCX/RDX/R8/R9 shadow slots. That 'seemingly useless over-allocation' is the MS x64 ABI shadow space.

questions.q: Under the Microsoft x64 ABI, where must a fifth argument be placed before the call?
choices: On the stack, just after (at a higher address than) the 0x20-byte shadow store
In R10
In the first slot of the shadow store
On the stack, below the return address in the callee's frame
questions.explain: 'Any parameters beyond the first four must be stored on the stack after the shadow store before the call.' In TooManyParameters, main does mov qword ptr [rsp+20h],55h: rsp+0 through rsp+1Fh is the shadow store, so arg 5 lands at rsp+20h.

questions.q: Within the shadow store, which register's slot sits at the lowest address, right above the return address?
choices: RCX
RDX
R8
R9
questions.explain: Going up from the return address, the slots are RCX (arg1), RDX, R8, then R9. That is consistent with the leftmost argument being at the lowest address.

questions.q: Per Microsoft's stack-usage documentation, how many parameter entries does a function A reserve for the functions it calls?
choices: Four, or the largest number of parameters taken by any function A calls, whichever is greater
Exactly four, always
The number of parameters A itself takes
Six, to match the System V register count
questions.explain: A reserves one area for both the register-parameter homes (RCX, RDX, R8, R9) and any stack parameters. It is sized for at least four entries, or more if some callee takes more.

questions.q: Pass1Parameter (VS x64): func's first instruction is mov dword ptr [rsp+8],ecx, executed BEFORE its sub rsp,18h. Where does that write land?
choices: In main's frame: the RCX shadow slot just above func's return address, outside func's own frame
In func's own local-variable area
On top of func's return address
In the 16-byte alignment padding at the top of main's frame
questions.explain: On entry, rsp points at the return address, so rsp+8 is the first shadow slot main reserved. The diagram shows a = ecx = 0x11 at 0x14FDE0, just above the return address at 0x14FDD8.

questions.q: After func executes sub rsp,18h, it reads its parameter with mov eax,dword ptr [rsp+20h]. Why +20h rather than +8?
choices: rsp moved down by 0x18, so the slot that was [rsp+8] is now [rsp+0x18+8] = [rsp+0x20]
The parameter was moved to a different slot during the subtraction
0x20 is the size of the shadow store, and parameters always come after it
The return address grew from 8 bytes to 0x20 bytes
questions.explain: The memory didn't move, only rsp did. Any rsp-relative offset to existing data grows by the amount subtracted from rsp.

questions.q: Why did func storing its register-passed argument back onto the stack in Pass1Parameter look wasteful?
choices: Passing in a register avoids memory, and writing it to the stack touches cache/RAM, which is much slower than register access
It overwrites main's return address
It doubles the number of instructions in main
Registers can't hold 32-bit values, so the store truncates the argument
questions.explain: In the memory hierarchy, registers are much faster than cache or RAM. Spilling the argument seems to defeat the speed benefit of register passing. The behavior turns out to be the MS shadow-store convention.

questions.q: TooManyParameters (VS x64): func(a,b,c,d,e) first spills r9, r8, rdx, rcx to [rsp+20h], [rsp+18h], [rsp+10h], [rsp+8], then does sub rsp,18h. Which parameter does sub rax,qword ptr [rsp+40h] subtract?
choices: e
d
c
a
questions.explain: After the sub, a is at 0x20, b at 0x28, c at 0x30 and d at 0x38. e was stored by main at its [rsp+20h], which is [rsp+28h] at func entry (the call pushed the return address) and 0x28+0x18 = 0x40 after the sub.

questions.q: In that same func, after sub rsp,18h, which C parameter is read by mov rax,qword ptr [rsp+28h]? (give the parameter name)
questions.explain: RDX (b) was spilled to [rsp+10h] before the sub, and 0x10 + 0x18 = 0x28.

questions.q: func computes i = a+b-c+d-e with a..e = 0x11, 0x22, 0x33, 0x44, 0x55. What is i as a signed decimal integer?
questions.explain: 17 + 34 - 51 + 68 - 85 = -17. The stack diagram shows it as ffffffef in i's 32-bit slot (two's complement).

questions.q: In TooManyParameters, main begins with sub rsp,38h. Which breakdown matches the stack diagram?
choices: 0x20 shadow store + 8 for the 5th argument + 8 undefined + 8 alignment padding
0x28 for the five arguments + 0x10 for locals
0x30 shadow store for six registers + 8 padding
0x20 shadow store + 0x18 for main's local variables
questions.explain: From high to low addresses, main's 0x38 bytes hold 16-byte-alignment padding, an undef slot, arg5 = 0x55, then the four shadow slots (r9, r8, rdx, rcx). That is 7 x 8 = 0x38.

questions.q: In the VS x64 TooManyParameters main, the fifth argument 0x55 is placed on the stack with a push instruction.
questions.explain: main uses mov qword ptr [rsp+20h],55h. Stack arguments are 'pushed' only notionally; compilers typically use mov into pre-allocated space.

questions.q: In the 32-bit cdecl convention (the default for most C code), who removes the pushed arguments from the stack after the call?
choices: The caller
The callee
The operating system
Nobody; they remain until the program exits
questions.explain: Under cdecl the caller always cleans up: if you push the parameters, you remove them.

questions.q: stdcall is used by Windows' Win32 APIs. How does it differ from cdecl?
choices: The callee cleans up the stack instead of the caller
Arguments are pushed left to right instead of right to left
The first four arguments go in registers
It never uses a stack frame
questions.explain: With stdcall, the called Win32 API removes the arguments the caller pushed. (It's 'standard call', but not the standard.)

questions.q: Where are you most likely to find the form of ret that also adds an amount to the stack pointer as it returns?
choices: At the end of stdcall functions such as Win32 APIs, since the callee cleans up its own arguments
At the end of every cdecl function
Only in main()
In System V x86-64 code that passes more than six arguments
questions.explain: A stdcall callee is responsible for removing its stack arguments, so it uses the ret form that pops the return address and also adjusts the stack pointer.

questions.q: 32-bit TooManyParameters (ints): main pushes 55h, 44h, 33h, 22h, 11h, calls func, then executes add esp, X. What is X in decimal?
questions.explain: 5 arguments x 4 bytes = 20 bytes (0x14, so the instruction is add esp,14h). That's the cdecl caller cleaning up its own pushes.

questions.q: 32-bit function parameters are pushed right to left. Where does the leftmost (first) parameter end up?
choices: At the lowest address, closest to the return address
At the highest address, farthest from the return address
In ECX
Just below the callee's saved EBP
questions.explain: main pushes 55h first and 11h last, so a = 0x11 sits at the lowest address, right above the return address. The rightmost argument is highest.

questions.q: In the 32-bit func (after push ebp; mov ebp,esp), what does mov eax,dword ptr [ebp+8] load?
choices: The first parameter, a
The saved EBP
The return address
The local variable i
questions.explain: [ebp] holds the saved EBP and [ebp+4] the return address. Then [ebp+8] = a, +0Ch = b, +10h = c, +14h = d, +18h = e. The local i is at [ebp-4].

questions.q: In the 32-bit Visual Studio build of func, the push ecx right after mov ebp,esp saves ECX because it is a callee-save register.
questions.explain: It's a Visual Studio quirk for allocating one int's worth of space for the local variable i, which is then written at [ebp-4]. ECX is caller-save in 32-bit VS anyway.

questions.q: Microsoft's 32-bit fastcall convention passes the first two parameters in which registers?
choices: ECX and EDX
EAX and EBX
ESI and EDI
EDX and EAX
questions.explain: fastcall puts parameter 1 in ECX and parameter 2 in EDX; the rest go on the stack. It uses no stack frames (extra overhead would make it less fast), so it's like a limited version of the x86-64 convention.

questions.q: In the 32-bit TooManyParameters stack diagram, the five arguments above the return address are the Microsoft shadow space.
questions.explain: These are the normal 32-bit stack-passed arguments, not shadow space. The 32-bit build also makes no alignment attempts, so there is no padding.

questions.q: Which registers are callee-save in 32-bit Visual Studio code?
choices: EAX
EBX
ECX
ESI
EDI
EBP
questions.explain: In 32-bit VS, EAX, ECX and EDX are caller-save, and EBX, ESI, EDI and EBP are callee-save. As in 64-bit, System V differs only on ESI and EDI, which it treats as caller-save.

questions.q: cdecl and stdcall perform explicit stack frame linkage. What does each function do on entry?
choices: push ebp, then mov ebp,esp: save the caller's frame pointer and point ebp at that saved copy
mov ebp,esp, then push ebp
sub esp,20h to create shadow space
push esp, then mov esp,ebp
questions.explain: The old EBP (stack frame base pointer) is pushed, then ESP, which now points at that saved copy, is moved into EBP. The saved EBPs chain the frames together.

questions.q: With an EBP-based frame in 32-bit code, how are parameters and local variables typically referenced?
choices: Parameters as [ebp+offset], locals as [ebp-offset] (gcc sometimes uses [esp+offset] for locals)
Parameters as [ebp-offset], locals as [ebp+offset]
Both as [esp-offset]
Parameters through ECX/EDX, locals through [ebp+offset]
questions.explain: Parameters live above the saved EBP and return address (positive offsets). Locals live below the saved EBP (negative offsets).

questions.q: Why do the GCC/Clang 64-bit HelloWorld builds have a balanced push rbp / pop rbp while the Visual Studio build doesn't?
choices: System V compilers still set up frame pointers in the 32-bit style unless compile options tell them not to, while MS x64 code generally doesn't use a frame pointer
RBP is caller-save on System V, so GCC must save it
Visual Studio stores RBP in the shadow store instead of pushing it
GCC and Clang need RBP to hold the first argument
questions.explain: This is a difference between the MS and System V ABIs. RBP is callee-save in both.

questions.q: When is Visual Studio x64 code definitely required to use a frame pointer?
choices: When the function uses _alloca() to allocate stack space dynamically
Whenever the function has local variables
Whenever it calls a function with more than four parameters
Only in debug builds
questions.explain: Per Microsoft's docs, _alloca must be 16-byte aligned and also requires a frame pointer. A nonvolatile register must mark the base of the fixed part of the stack and be saved and initialized in the prolog.

questions.q: Microsoft's x64 documentation requires the frame pointer to be RBP specifically.
questions.explain: The docs only say 'a nonvolatile register'. One of Microsoft's own examples uses R13 instead of RBP.

questions.q: In the 64-bit Visual Studio 'maximum' stack diagram, what lies directly above (at a higher address than) the return address from foo() to main()?
choices: Shadow space plus any extra function arguments
Saved RBP
foo's local variables
Callee-save registers
questions.explain: From high to low addresses, main's frame holds locals, callee-save regs, caller-save regs, then shadow space + extra function arguments. The return address follows, and then foo's frame begins.

questions.q: In the 64-bit System V 'maximum' stack diagram, what is the first item placed in a function's own frame, which rbp is then made to point at?
choices: The saved rbp (the caller's frame pointer)
Shadow space
Callee-save registers
The function's return value
questions.explain: System V code does push rbp; mov rbp,rsp, just like the 32-bit ebp linkage. Locals, callee-save regs, caller-save regs and stack arguments follow below it.

questions.q: In the System V x86-64 stack layout, there is no shadow space: a frame goes from caller-save registers straight to any stack-passed function arguments and then the return address.
questions.explain: Shadow space is specific to the Microsoft x64 ABI. The System V diagram shows saved rbp, locals, callee-save, caller-save, function arguments (if any), then the return address.
